Risk: reviewers may lack MFRM/IRT background — need clear, self-contained exposition with toy examples. Strength: AAAI values formal modeling + practical impact.\\n- **ACL/ARR**: Good fit for LLM evaluation methodology. Risk: may demand stronger NLP-specific contributions beyond the measurement framework. Strength: directly relevant to LLM evaluation community.\\n\\n## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Responses\\n\\n1. **\\\"Why not CyclicJudge + discard contaminated items?\\\"** — Item discard wastes information; CyclicJudge doesn't capture item-specific judge effects; neither produces c_n for auditing; G-MFRM degrades gracefully to standard MFRM when contamination ≈ 0. Stage 2 external anchoring solves a fundamental obstacle (exposure unknown to administrator) absent in educational testing. Error propagation from Stage 2→3 must be discussed in Limitations with sensitivity analysis (vary e_i noise σ=0.1,0.2,0.5).\\n\\n4b. **\\\"Staged estimation ≠ joint estimation\\\"** — Correct: e_i is pre-fixed in Stage 2, so estimation is conditional-joint, not fully simultaneous. Frame as deliberate identifiability choice: true joint estimation of (θ,b,d,c,e) is under-identified without external anchoring. Staged estimation is the principled solution. Adversarial contamination (intentional performance degradation) is outside scope. Discuss in Limitations.\\n\\n8. **\\\"≥4 judges needed — too expensive?\\\"** — Leave-one-judge-out analysis during exp-003 fitting shows degradation curve as judge count decreases. Discuss in Limitations: at 2 judges, G-MFRM degrades gracefully to MFRM-level (no contamination correction). Cost-benefit analysis for practitioners.\\n\\n9. **\\\"No judge-model interaction term?\\\"** — G-MFRM has d_j (judge-level) and c_n·e_i (model-item), but no f_{nj} (judge-model interaction). Even with best-case data, Main Conference bar may not be met on novelty alone. Supplement with:\\n\\n1. **Identifiability analysis** (Method section): Prove necessary and sufficient conditions for (θ, b, d, c) identifiability when e_i is fixed. This is a non-trivial technical contribution beyond \\\"adding a term.\\\"\\n2. **Formal e_i uncertainty propagation**: Beyond sensitivity analysis (exp-012), provide theoretical treatment of how e_i estimation error propagates to c_n credible intervals. ## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 ARR (submission deadline May 26, 2026)
- Timeline: 4 days from today (2026-05-22)

## Core Insight
Sequential approaches to judge bias correction and contamination adjustment produce biased model ability estimates due to omitted variable confounding. Joint estimation within a single psychometric calibration framework is methodologically necessary, not merely convenient.

## Core Claims (3 条，均可证伪)

1. **Confounding Claim**: When judge severity (d_j) and contamination susceptibility (c_n·e_i) are both present but only one is modeled, the unmodeled facet's effect is absorbed into other parameter estimates, producing systematic bias in model ability rankings. Sequential pipelines (bias-first or contamination-first) do not resolve this confounding. (Note: OVB formalization supports this claim as mechanism explanation — "identify and quantify confounding in LLM evaluation" — not as independent theoretical contribution. Cite Angrist & Pischke 2009 as source.)

2. **Framework Claim**: The Gated Many-Facet Rasch Model (G-MFRM) — combining MFRM's multi-facet structure with DG-IRT's gating mechanism and externally-anchored exposure indicators — provides a staged joint calibration that estimates model ability, item difficulty, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility, yielding bias-and-contamination-corrected "fair scores." (Note: "staged joint" — e_i is pre-estimated in Stage 2 and fixed in Stage 3; the joint estimation is conditional on e_i. This is a deliberate identifiability choice, not fully simultaneous. Paper must use "staged joint calibration" or "conditional joint estimation," never "fully joint.")

3. **Empirical Claim**: G-MFRM fair scores achieve higher agreement with human rankings (Chatbot Arena votes, Kendall-τ) than all baselines: raw multi-judge averages, bias-only correction (CyclicJudge, UDA), contamination-only adjustment (DCR), and naive sequential pipelines.

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation has bifurcated into two correction silos — judge bias and benchmark contamination — that are addressed independently. But judge severity and contamination effects are confounded: bias-only methods absorb contamination inflation into ability estimates; contamination-only methods misattribute judge effects as contamination signals. Sequential correction cannot resolve this because the first stage's estimates are already biased by the unmodeled facet.

- **Existing approaches & gaps**: CyclicJudge eliminates average judge bias via round-robin but ignores contamination. UDA uses neural K-factor adjustment (−63.4% inter-judge std) but is black-box and contamination-unaware. DCR/ConStat quantify contamination effects (r²=0.94) but ignore judge variation. In LLM evaluation literature, no existing work jointly models both within a single calibration framework. (Note: educational measurement has MFRM+DIF joint modeling — Eckes 2011, Patz et al. 2002, Fox & Glas 2001, Wind & Peterson 2018 — but these address test fairness, not LLM contamination. G-MFRM is the first to apply continuous-exposure gating within MFRM for LLM evaluation. "First" claim must be precisely scoped to LLM evaluation with continuous exposure.)

- **Our framing**: Joint estimation is methodologically necessary. We formalize this as an omitted variable bias problem: under non-orthogonality of d_j and c_n·e_i, sequential estimators are asymptotically biased (direction determined by covariance sign). G-MFRM resolves this by estimating all facets simultaneously, with a three-stage procedure ensuring identifiability: (1) standard MFRM for initial estimates, (2) external per-item exposure estimation via item-level performance gap (original vs reference variants) with difficulty correction, supplemented by temporal signals and LogProber where available, (3) joint gated model with e_i fixed and c_n as latent parameters. ConStat per-model delta serves as external validation of fitted c_n.

- **MCMC Implementation Note (Method section)**: Use NCP for c_n to avoid funnel geometries. Centered parameterization yields ESS~47 vs 224+ with NCP. Report convergence diagnostics (R̂ < 1.05, ESS > 100). One sentence + footnote in paper, not a subsection.

- **Headline result template**: "On MT-Bench/Arena-Hard with 8 LLM judges, G-MFRM fair scores achieve X% higher Kendall-τ with Chatbot Arena human votes than the best sequential baseline, while simultaneously producing interpretable per-model contamination estimates and per-judge severity profiles."

## Narrative Strategy (from distilled writing)

- **Type**: "突破局限" (sequential has structural flaw) + "统一框架" (G-MFRM unifies both corrections)
- **Opening hook**: Quantitative shock — lead with confounding's θ-RMSE degradation (43.8% in synthetic, to be validated on real data)
- **Section 2**: Toy example / formal **observation** (NOT "proposition" — this is standard OVB from Angrist & Pischke 2009 applied to LLM evaluation; cite originals, present as domain-specific instantiation) demonstrating confounding before introducing G-MFRM method
- **Figure 1**: Left = sequential pipeline with confounding annotation, Right = joint G-MFRM with gating mechanism highlighted
- **Main result table**: rows = methods (7 baselines + G-MFRM), cols = benchmarks × metrics
- **Ablation**: Full numbers (not checkmark grid), rows = components on/off

## Venue Fit Risks

- **AAAI**: Good fit for psychometric methodology applied to AI evaluation. Risk: reviewers may lack MFRM/IRT background — need clear, self-contained exposition with toy examples. Strength: AAAI values formal modeling + practical impact.
- **ACL/ARR**: Good fit for LLM evaluation methodology. Risk: may demand stronger NLP-specific contributions beyond the measurement framework. Strength: directly relevant to LLM evaluation community.

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Responses

1. **"Why not CyclicJudge + discard contaminated items?"** — Item discard wastes information; CyclicJudge doesn't capture item-specific judge effects; neither produces c_n for auditing; G-MFRM degrades gracefully to standard MFRM when contamination ≈ 0. Synthetic validation confirms graceful degradation: under weak contamination (c~HalfNormal(0.5), ρ=0.0), G-MFRM shows no significant degradation vs sequential (non-degradation p=0.96), demonstrating that gating parameters do not introduce noise when signal is absent.

2. **"Is confounding large enough in practice?"** — MVP synthetic: 43.8% RMSE degradation. Real-data calibration (P0 experiment) will establish realistic contamination magnitude. Bias scatter (r=0.65) shows the mechanism exists regardless of magnitude.

3. **"Rank-1 assumption (c_n·e_i) too strong"** — Rank-1 is LLTM tradition, good approximation when contamination comes from dominant data source. Person-fit diagnostics (infit/outfit) detect violations. Rank-k extension is future work.

4. **"DG-IRT transfer is trivial"** — Three structural differences require non-trivial adaptation: binary→continuous exposure, single-rater→multi-facet, known→unknown exposure status. Stage 2 external anchoring solves a fundamental obstacle (exposure unknown to administrator) absent in educational testing. Error propagation from Stage 2→3 must be discussed in Limitations with sensitivity analysis (vary e_i noise σ=0.1,0.2,0.5).

4b. **"Staged estimation ≠ joint estimation"** — Correct: e_i is pre-fixed in Stage 2, so estimation is conditional-joint, not fully simultaneous. Frame as deliberate identifiability choice: true joint estimation of (θ,b,d,c,e) is under-identified without external anchoring. Staged estimation is the principled solution. Compare to two-step estimators in econometrics (Heckman 1979). exp-012 establishes explicit applicability bounds: robust at σ_e ≤ σ_crit ≈ √Var(e_i) (θ +5.9% at σ=0.2), degrades beyond (θ +36.9% at σ=0.5). This testable boundary makes the staged approximation falsifiable — a methodological strength, not weakness.

5. **"Contamination signal realistic?"** — ConStat validated r²=0.94 with true contamination effects. LogProber provides per-item memorization indicators. Multiple indicators combined via weighted composite. P0 experiment calibrates against real benchmarks.

6. **"Chatbot Arena Elo as ground truth — circular reasoning?"** — Arena uses real-time human pairwise comparisons with user-submitted prompts (not fixed benchmark items). Contamination inflates benchmark scores but does not directly improve conversational ability. Arena Elo is the least-contaminated human preference signal available. Acknowledge limitation in paper but argue decoupling is strong.

7. **"c_n ≥ 0 assumption too restrictive?"** — Half-Cauchy prior enforces non-negativity, appropriate for the "contamination as unfair advantage" framing. Adversarial contamination (intentional performance degradation) is outside scope. Discuss in Limitations.

8. **"≥4 judges needed — too expensive?"** — Leave-one-judge-out analysis during exp-003 fitting shows degradation curve as judge count decreases. Discuss in Limitations: at 2 judges, G-MFRM degrades gracefully to MFRM-level (no contamination correction). Cost-benefit analysis for practitioners.

9. **"No judge-model interaction term?"** — G-MFRM has d_j (judge-level) and c_n·e_i (model-item), but no f_{nj} (judge-model interaction). Preference Leakage shows same-model PLS≈23.6%, same-family≈8.9%. When GPT-5.5 judges GPT-5.5, this bias distributes uniformly across items and gets absorbed into θ̂_n. Mitigation: (a) leave-one-judge-out residual analysis during exp-003 fitting detects if specific judges inflate same-family models; (b) Limitations section acknowledges scope boundary; (c) rank-k extension with judge-model interaction is future work.

The bilinear term also assumes rank-1 structure---a single contamination dimension per model---while contamination may be domain-specific (e.g., coding vs.\ reasoning), requiring a higher-rank decomposition $\sum_r c_{nr} \cdot e_{ir}$ that the current model does not capture.

The evaluation uses a single benchmark (Arena-Hard) with XX.X\% fill rate (XX{,}XXX of XX{,}XXX potential cells); sparser designs may compromise identifiability of $c_n$ for models with few observed exposed items, and sparse per-item observations produce elevated item-level mean-square residuals (92/176 items), though model- and judge-level fit remains acceptable. Stage~2 exposure estimation relies on a reference model anchor (gpt-4-0314), whose validity should be periodically re-assessed as benchmarks age.

Empirical CI coverage differs by parameter type: ability estimates $\theta$ approach nominal coverage (${\sim}$90\% at $N = 8$), while contamination susceptibility $c_n$ exhibits posterior overconfidence (71\% at $N = 50$, 68\% at $N = 8$; \citealp{talts2018sbc}), a structural issue from the multiplicative coupling $c_n \cdot e_i$ and the HalfNormal boundary constraint at $c_n = 0$ that does not improve with sample size; $c_n$ credible intervals should be treated as lower bounds on uncertainty (Appendix~\ref{app:ci_coverage}), with SBC-based recalibration as a direction for future work. The bilinear term also assumes rank-1 structure---a single contamination dimension per model---while contamination may be domain-specific (e.g., coding vs.\ reasoning), requiring a higher-rank decomposition $\sum_r c_{nr} \cdot e_{ir}$ that the current model does not capture.

Post-hoc power analysis indicates $N \approx 17$ for 80\% power to detect $\Delta\tau = 0.071$; the $N = 8$ evaluation has ${\sim}$50\% power, explaining the non-significant bootstrap result. Generalization to other benchmarks and larger model populations remains to be verified. While self-evaluation sensitivity analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:self_eval}) confirms robust rankings when excluding self-judging observations, removing overlapping models entirely from the judge panel has not been conducted.

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Data and models.} We evaluate on Arena-Hard \citep{li2024arenahard}, a benchmark of 316 multi-turn conversational items selected for high separability among frontier models. After filtering for coverage, the evaluation set comprises 176 items in a connected incomplete design (XX{,}XXX observations; XX.X\% fill rate of the full $N \times I \times J$ tensor). Seventeen target models spanning proprietary and open-source families are evaluated: the original 8 models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-72B, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-2-9B, GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-Turbo) plus 9 additional models (Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4-Turbo, LLaMA-3.1-70B, Gemma-2-27B, Claude-3-Opus, LLaMA-3-70B, Mixtral-8x22B, Claude-3-Haiku, LLaMA-3-8B). Ground-truth rankings are derived from Chatbot Arena human preference data \citep{zheng2023mtbench}.
8	
9	\paragraph{Judges.} Nine LLM judges score model responses in position-swapped pairwise mode: GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Mistral-Large-2, LLaMA-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, and Qwen3-235B. Seven judges cover all 17 target models; two judges (GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7) cover only the original 8 models, yielding an asymmetric connected design---Theorem~\ref{thm:sufficient} requires only connectivity, not full crossing. Position swapping controls for position bias and doubles the effective observation count. Two models---Qwen2.5-72B and LLaMA-3.3-70B---serve as both judge and target; $d_j$ absorbs systematic self-evaluation bias, and excluding self-judging observations leaves rankings unchanged ($\tau = 0.857$; Appendix~\ref{app:self_eval}).
10	
11	\paragraph{Exposure estimation.} Per-item exposure $e_i$ is estimated via a two-source pipeline (\S\ref{sec:staged}): reference model anchoring with gpt-4-0314 as anchor (75\% weight) and cross-model agreement (25\% weight). The pipeline is robust to weight configuration (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.998$ across all configurations tested).
12	
13	\paragraph{MCMC.} We use NumPyro NUTS with 4{,}000 warmup and 4{,}000 sampling iterations across 4 chains (target acceptance 0.95). The contamination prior follows the hierarchical HalfNormal specification (Eq.~\ref{eq:contam_prior}). Convergence is assessed via rank-normalized split-$\hat{R}$ \citep{vehtari2021rhat} with conventional $\hat{R} < 1.05$ and ESS $> 100$ thresholds \citep{gelman2013bda}.
14	
15	\subsection{Baselines and Main Results}
16	\label{sec:main_results}
17	
18	We compare G-MFRM against seven methods that address judge bias or contamination separately: (1) Raw Average, (2) MFRM-only (Eq.~\ref{eq:mfrm}), (3) Sequential pipeline (MFRM then contamination adjustment), (4) CyclicJudge \citep{cyclicjudge2026}, (5) CyclicJudge+discard (exposed items removed), (6) DCR Factor \citep{dcr2025}, and (7) Preference Leakage calibration \citep{preference_leakage2026}. All methods are evaluated by Kendall $\tau$ and Spearman $\rho$ against Chatbot Arena human rankings.
19	
20	\begin{table}[t]
21	\centering
22	\small
23	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
24	\toprule
25	& \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{8 models}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{17 models}} \\
26	\cmidrule(lr){2-3} \cmidrule(lr){4-5}
27	\textbf{Method} & $\tau$ & $\rho$ & $\tau$ & $\rho$ \\
28	\midrule
29	Raw Average & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
30	MFRM-only & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
31	Sequential & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
32	CyclicJudge & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
33	CyclicJudge+discard & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
34	DCR Factor & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
35	Pref.\ Leakage & 0.786 & 0.905 & TBD & TBD \\
36	\midrule
37	G-MFRM (ours) & \textbf{0.857} & \textbf{0.952} & \textbf{TBD} & \textbf{TBD} \\
38	\bottomrule
39	\end{tabular}
40	\caption{Correlation with Chatbot Arena human rankings on Arena-Hard (9 judges). All seven baselines produce identical rankings at $N = 8$ ($\tau = 0.786$). G-MFRM yields nominally higher point-estimate rank agreement ($+$7.1pp; bootstrap $\Delta\tau$ CI includes zero). Right columns report the 17-model evaluation (TBD).}
41	\label{tab:main_results}
42	\end{table}
43	
44	All seven baselines produce identical model rankings ($\tau = 0.786$, $\rho = 0.905$). With $N = 8$, Kendall $\tau$ takes only ${\sim}20$ distinct values, but raw ability scores also vary by $< 0.03$ logits across methods (Table~\ref{tab:raw_scores}), confirming genuine invariance rather than discretization artifact. This reflects the structural confounding from Section~\ref{sec:confounding}: single-facet corrections leave the uncorrected confound intact (Observation~\ref{obs:ovb}). That CyclicJudge+discard also preserves rankings suggests contamination effects on aggregate rankings are modest at this scale; G-MFRM's primary value lies in per-model contamination diagnostics. G-MFRM achieves nominally higher point-estimate rank agreement ($\tau = 0.857$, $\rho = 0.952$) over the baselines ($\tau = 0.786$), but the posterior median $\tau$ equals the baseline (0.786), with the point estimate at the distribution's upper tail. Bootstrap resampling (4{,}000 posterior draws) yields $\Delta\tau$ 95\% CI $[-0.071, 0.071]$: the ranking improvement is not statistically significant at $N = 8$, though G-MFRM almost never degrades rankings ($P(\Delta\tau \geq 0) = 0.927$). On synthetic data ($N = 50$), joint estimation significantly outperforms sequential ($\tau = 0.922$ vs.\ $0.839$, Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$), confirming that the effect is real but below detection at this sample size. The rank change---gpt-4o-mini and qwen2.5-72b swap positions---is consistent with differential contamination ($P(\theta_{\text{mini}} > \theta_{\text{qwen}}) = 0.853$).
45	
46	We evaluate G-MFRM along two orthogonal axes: predictive fit and ranking accuracy.
47	
48	\paragraph{Predictive fit.} LOO cross-validation strongly favors G-MFRM ($\Delta\mathrm{ELPD}_{\mathrm{LOO}} = -55.7$, SE $= 9.4$, $|\Delta/\mathrm{SE}| = 5.9$; \citealp{vehtari2017loo}), with stacking weight 1.0 for G-MFRM versus 0.0 for MFRM-only. All Pareto $\hat{k} < 0.7$, confirming reliable LOO estimates. The contamination gating term substantially improves held-out predictive fit.
49	
50	\paragraph{Ranking accuracy.} Ranking improvement ($\Delta\tau = +0.071$) is not statistically significant at $N = 8$ (bootstrap 95\% CI crosses zero). Post-hoc power analysis indicates $N \approx 17$ is needed for 80\% power to detect this effect size (Appendix~\ref{app:power}). This prediction is empirically validated: at $N = 20$, synthetic $\Delta\tau$ reaches significance (Wilcoxon $p < 0.001$, 18 wins / 1 loss; Appendix~\ref{app:synthetic_calibration}). Pooling 20 replications at $N = 8$ also yields significance ($p < 0.002$), confirming the method consistently improves rankings though any single $N = 8$ dataset has limited power.
51	
52	The MCMC sampler achieves rank-normalized split-$\hat{R} \leq 1.03$ across all parameters with zero divergent transitions and minimum bulk ESS of 174 and minimum tail ESS of 381 (model-level parameters: bulk ESS $\geq$ 217, tail ESS $\geq$ 437). These values satisfy the traditional convergence thresholds ($\hat{R} < 1.05$, ESS $> 100$; \citealp{gelman2013bda}) but do not meet the stricter criteria of \citet{vehtari2021rhat} ($\hat{R} < 1.01$, ESS $> 400$), which may contribute to posterior overconfidence (synthetic CI coverage 71\%; see Limitations); we report point estimates and rank orderings as primary results. Model and judge facets show acceptable fit (all infit/outfit MNSQ within $[0.63, 1.07]$; item-level diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:item_diagnostics}). Posterior predictive checks confirm adequate model fit (predicted response rate $0.593$ vs.\ observed $0.599$; Appendix~\ref{app:ppc}). Contamination susceptibility $\hat{c}_n$ exhibits a gradient by model age, directionally consistent with known training data exposure (Appendix~\ref{app:cn_recovery}). Estimated $\hat{c}_n$ exceeds 1.0 for the four oldest models: GPT-3.5-Turbo ($\hat{c}_n = 5.60$), GPT-4-0613 ($4.20$), Qwen2.5-72B ($3.00$), and LLaMA-3.3-70B ($2.50$). The most recent models show low estimated contamination: GPT-4o ($0.88$) and GPT-4o-mini ($0.93$). The global shrinkage scale $\hat{\sigma}_c = 2.40$ confirms substantial inter-model heterogeneity ($\bar{c} = 2.50$, aligning with the strong-contamination regime in synthetic validation). Notably, sequential estimation yields near-zero contamination estimates ($\bar{c} \approx 0$), demonstrating that without joint modeling, contamination effects are entirely absorbed into ability estimates $\hat{\theta}$---precisely the omitted variable bias predicted by the theoretical analysis (Section~\ref{sec:confounding}). A per-model diagnostic (Table~\ref{tab:bias_absorption}) reveals that MFRM-only inflates ability estimates for the most contaminated models by up to 0.79 logits (GPT-3.5-Turbo), while deflating estimates for the least contaminated models by up to 0.40 logits (GPT-4o). Judge severity $d_j$ separates by provenance: proprietary judges tend to score more strictly (e.g., Claude Opus $+0.60$, GPT-5.5 $+0.53$) than open-source judges (e.g., Mistral $-0.74$, LLaMA $-0.42$); full $d_j$ values for all nine judges are reported in Table~\ref{tab:judge_severity}. Results are robust to prior specification (Horseshoe \citep{piironen2017horseshoe} vs.\ HalfNormal: Pearson $r > 0.999$; Appendix~\ref{app:prior_robustness}) and to judge panel size: G-MFRM outperforms baselines at all judge counts $k \geq 2$, with $\tau$ increasing monotonically from $0.771$ ($k = 2$) to $0.857$ ($k = 9$); $k \geq 4$ suffices to exceed the full-panel baseline (Appendix~\ref{app:judge_count}).
53	
54	\subsection{Error Propagation Robustness}
55	\label{sec:error_prop_results}
56	
57	Section~\ref{sec:error_prop} predicted that ability estimates degrade gracefully when exposure noise $\sigma$ remains below $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(e_i)} \approx 0.2$. We validate this prediction by injecting Gaussian noise into the true exposure values and re-fitting G-MFRM on synthetic data ($N = 50$, $I = 100$, $J = 8$, 20 seeds; exp-012).
58	
59	\begin{table}[t]
60	\centering
61	\small
62	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
63	\toprule
64	$\sigma$ & $\theta$-RMSE & $\Delta\theta$\% & $c_n$-RMSE & $\Delta c_n$\% \\
65	\midrule
66	0.0 & 0.128 $\pm$ 0.018 & --- & 0.533 $\pm$ 0.187 & --- \\
67	0.1 & 0.130 $\pm$ 0.018 & +1.4 & 0.545 $\pm$ 0.192 & +2.3 \\
68	0.2 & 0.135 $\pm$ 0.018 & +5.9 & 0.575 $\pm$ 0.198 & +7.9 \\
69	0.5 & 0.175 $\pm$ 0.027 & +36.9 & 0.842 $\pm$ 0.281 & +57.9 \\
70	\bottomrule
71	\end{tabular}
72	\caption{Error propagation robustness (exp-012). Ability RMSE degrades by less than 6\% when exposure noise $\sigma \leq 0.2$, matching the theoretical prediction. Contamination estimates are more sensitive due to multiplicative coupling with $e_i$.}
73	\label{tab:error_prop}
74	\end{table}
75	
76	Table~\ref{tab:error_prop} confirms this prediction: below $\sigma = 0.2$, ability RMSE increases by 5.9\% and contamination RMSE by 7.9\%; beyond the threshold ($\sigma = 0.5$), degradation becomes substantial. Rank ordering is preserved even at $\sigma = 0.5$ ($\tau > 0.88$).
77	
78	Ablation (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}, Appendix) confirms joint estimation as the dominant contributor: staged estimation increases $\theta$-RMSE by $2.0\times$ ($p < 0.001$); continuous gating improves $c_n$-RMSE by 40\% over binary ($p < 0.001$). Removing $d_j$ preserves rankings but degrades contamination recovery ($c_n$-RMSE $+$6\%, $p < 0.001$).
